blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Inconsistency in ampere circuital law: The source of a magnetic field is not just the conduction electric current due to flowing charges, but also the time rate of change of electric field.

1.Conduction current  $\left(\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{c}}\right)$

  • Due to flow of charge in the conducting wire.
$\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{c}}=\frac{\mathrm{dq}}{\mathrm{dt}}$

2.Displacement current $\left(\mathbf{I}_{\mathrm{d}}\right)$

  • Due to variable electric field between plates of charging capacitor.
  • $\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{D}}=\epsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi_{\mathrm{E}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$
Hence, total current is defined as $\mathrm{I}=\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{C}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}$

So, Ampere's Circuital Law can be written as $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \overrightarrow{\mathrm{l}}=\mu_0\left(\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{c}}+\mathrm{I}_{\mathrm{d}}\right)$  [Also known as Ampere Maxwell's Law]

Note: Displacement current also solved the current continuity problem

Maxwell Equations

1.  $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{d\overrightarrow{A}}=\frac{\mathrm{Q}}{\varepsilon_0}$ (Gauss's law of Electrostatics)

2.  $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \mathrm{d \overrightarrow{A}}=0$ (Gauss's law of magnetism)

3. $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \cdot \mathrm{~d}  \overrightarrow{\ell}=-\frac{\mathrm{d} \phi_{\mathrm{B}}}{\mathrm{dt}}$ (Maxwell - Faraday's Law)

4. $\oint \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}} \cdot \mathrm{~d} \boldsymbol{ \overrightarrow{l}}=\mu_0\left[\mathrm{i}_{\mathrm{c}}+\varepsilon_0 \frac{\mathrm{~d} \phi_{\mathrm{E}}}{\mathrm{dt}}\right]$ (Ampere - Maxwell Law)

blocks.title: Core Concept
blocks.text:
Electromagnetic waves consist of sinusoidally time varying Electric and Magnetic fields. Electric and magnetic fields oscillate sinusoidally in  perpendicular planes as well as the direction the propagation of waves, so EMW are transverse in nature.

Electromagnetic Spectrum

Properties of Electromagnetic Waves:

1.EMW are non-mechanical in nature, and they don’t require medium to transfer energy and momentum.

2.The electric and magnetic fields variations are in phase.

3.The direction of propagation of wave is along $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}}$.

4.The electric and magnetic fields of a sinusoidal electromagnetic wave propagating in the positive x-direction can be written as

$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{Y}}=\mathrm{E}_0 \sin (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t}) \\ & \mathrm{B}_{\mathrm{Z}}=\mathrm{B}_0 \sin (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t}) \end{aligned}$

5.The magnitude of the electric and the magnetic fields in an electromagnetic wave are related as  $\dfrac{E}{B}=v \text { For free space, } \frac{E}{B}=C$.

6.$\text { In vacuum, speed of EMW is } c=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}}=3 \times 10^8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

7.$\text { In medium : } \mathrm{v}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\mu_0 \mu_{\mathrm{r}}\right)\left(\varepsilon_0 \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}\right)}}=\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\mu_0 \varepsilon_0\right)}} \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{\left(\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}\right)}}=\frac{\mathrm{c}}{\sqrt{\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}}}$

8.Refractive index, $\mathrm{n}=\dfrac{\mathrm{c}}{\mathrm{v}}=\sqrt{\left(\mu_{\mathrm{r}} \varepsilon_{\mathrm{r}}\right)}$

9.$\text { Like any other wave, } \mathrm{c}=\mathrm{f} \lambda \text { is applicable for EMW as well. }$

blocks.title: Example-1
blocks.question:
In an electromagnetic wave in free space the root mean square value of the electric field is $E_{r m s}=6 \mathrm{~V} / \mathrm{m}$. The peak value of the magnetic field is :-

(1) $2.83 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~T}$

(2) $0.70 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~T}$

(3) $4.23 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~T}$

(4) $1.41 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~T}$
blocks.answer:
Ans. (1)

$\begin{aligned} & E_0=c B_0 \\ & E_{\text {rms }}=\frac{E_0}{\sqrt{2}} \\ & \Rightarrow E_{\text {mrs }} \sqrt{2}=c B_0 \\ & \Rightarrow B_0=\frac{E_{\mathrm{rms}} \sqrt{2}}{c}=\frac{6 \times \sqrt{2}}{3 \times 10^8}=2.83 \times 10^{-8} \mathrm{~T} \end{aligned}$

blocks.title: Core Concepts
blocks.text:
Energy Density

Total Energy Density = Energy Density in Electric Field + Energy Density in Magnetic Field

$\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{T}}=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{E}^2+\frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~B}^2}{\mu_0}$

$\text { Where, } \begin{aligned} \mathrm{E} & =\mathrm{E}_0 \sin (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t}) \\ \mathrm{B} & =\mathrm{B}_0 \sin (\mathrm{kx}-\omega \mathrm{t}) \end{aligned}$

We know that, For Free Space,

$c=\frac{E}{B} \& c=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}} \Rightarrow \frac{E^2}{B^2}=\frac{1}{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}$

$\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{E}}=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{E}^2=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0\left(\frac{\mathrm{~B}^2}{\mu_0 \varepsilon_0}\right)=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~B}^2}{\mu_0}=\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{B}}$

Average Energy Density

(a) Average Energy Density of Electric Field

$<\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{E}}>=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0\left(\frac{\mathrm{E}_0^2}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{4} \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{E}_0^2$

(B) Average Energy Density of Magnetic Field

$<\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{B}}>=\frac{1}{2} \frac{1}{\mu_0}\left(\frac{\mathrm{~B}_0^2}{2}\right)=\frac{1}{4} \frac{\mathrm{~B}_0^2}{\mu_0}$

Average Energy Density of Electromagnetic Wave

$<\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{T}}>=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{E}_0^2=\frac{1}{2} \frac{\mathrm{~B}_0^2}{\mu_0}$

$\text { Unit: } \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{m}^3$

$E_0 \& B_0 \text { are peak values. }$

Poynting Vector : The total energy flowing perpendicularly per second per unit area into the surface in free space is called a Poynting Vector. It also represents instantaneous  power transferred per unit area.

Direction : Along direction of wave propagation

$\text { SI unit: } \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{s}-\mathrm{m}^2 \text { or } \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^2$

$\overrightarrow{\mathrm{S}}=\frac{1}{\mu_0}(\overrightarrow{\mathrm{E}} \times \overrightarrow{\mathrm{B}})$

$\mathrm{S}=\frac{\mathrm{EB}}{\mu_0}=\frac{\mathrm{E}^2}{\mathrm{c} \mu_0}=\frac{\mathrm{B}^2 \mathrm{c}}{\mu_0}$

Intensity :  It represents the average time rate at which energy flows through a unit surface area perpendicular to the direction of the propagation of the wave. In other words, it is the average value of poynting vector over one cycle. It also represents average power transferred per unit area.

Direction : Along direction of wave propagation.

$\text { SI unit : } \mathrm{J} / \mathrm{s}-\mathrm{m}^2 \text { or } \mathrm{W} / \mathrm{m}^2$

$\mathrm{I}=\langle\mathrm{S}\rangle=\mathrm{c}\langle\mathrm{U}\rangle=\mathrm{c} \frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{E}_{\mathrm{o}}^2=\mathrm{c} \frac{\mathrm{~B}_{\mathrm{o}}^2}{2 \mu_{\mathrm{o}}}$

Momentum of Electromagnetic Waves :  The linear momentum carried by the portion of wave having energy U is given by  $p=\frac{U}{c}$

Radiation Pressure : The mechanical pressure exerted upon any surface due to the exchange of momentum between the surface and the electromagnetic wave.

$\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{\mathrm{F}}{\mathrm{~A}}$

Transfer of Momentum and Radiation Pressure :-

CASE(1) : If section of an EMW having energy U strikes a surface of surface area A, then if the surface is perfect absorber and incidence is normal then momentum transferred to the surface,

$\Delta \mathrm{p}=\frac{\mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{c}}$

Force exerted on the surface by EMW

$\text { Radiation Pressure, } \mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{c}}$

CASE-(2) : If section of an EMW having energy U strikes a surface of surface area A, then if the surface is perfect reflector and incidence is normal then momentum transferred to the surface,

$\Delta \mathrm{p}=\frac{2 \mathrm{U}}{\mathrm{c}}$

Radiation pressure  $\mathrm{P}_{\mathrm{R}}=\frac{2 \mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{c}}$

blocks.title: Example-2
blocks.question: A plane light wave in the visible region is moving along the Z-direction. The frequency of the wave is $0.5 \times 10^{15}$ Hz and the electric field at any point is varying sinusoidally with time with an amplitude of 1 V/m. Calculate the energy densities of the electric and magnetic fields.
blocks.answer:
Total average energy density (due to both electric and magnetic fields)

$\left\langle\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{T}}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{2} \varepsilon_0 \mathrm{E}_0^2=\frac{1}{2}\left(8.85 \times 10^{-12}\right)(1)^2=4.42 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^3$

Since the energy is shared equally by the electric and magnetic fields, average energy density of the electric field

$\left\langle\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{E}}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{2}\left(4.42 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^3\right)=2.21 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^3$

average energy density of the magnetic field

$<\mathrm{U}_{\mathrm{B}}>=\frac{1}{2}\left(4.42 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^3\right)=2.21 \times 10^{-12} \mathrm{~J} / \mathrm{m}^3$

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Neglecting the Displacement Current: Ignoring the term $\varepsilon_0 \frac{\partial E}{\partial \mathrm{t}}$​ in time-varying electric fields.

2. Misapplying Ampere’s Law to Dynamic Situations: Using the static form of Ampere’s Law without accounting for changing electric fields.

3. Incorrect Symmetry Assumptions: Misinterpreting symmetry, leading to wrong field assumptions in time-varying situations.

4. Ignoring Boundary Conditions: Overlooking conditions at material interfaces, which can affect displacement currents.

5. Wrong Use of Integral Form: Failing to include both free and displacement currents when applying Ampere’s Law in integral form.

blocks.title: Common Mistakes
blocks.text:
1. Confusing Frequency and Wavelength: Misunderstanding their relationship $(c=f \lambda) .$

2. Ignoring Medium Properties: Not accounting for how waves change in different materials.

3. Incorrect Wave Equation Use: Applying wrong wave equations, especially in non-vacuum media.

4. Misunderstanding the Spectrum: Confusing the different regions of the electromagnetic spectrum and their properties.

blocks.text:
